30 What is equivalent to one volt?
A
one coulomb per second
B
one joule per coulomb
C
one joule per second
D
one joule second per coulomb squared

hints: Notice the question asks about the volt, the unit of potential difference, which links energy transferred $W$ in joules to charge $Q$ in coulombs.
Recall the defining relation $V = W/Q$, so think about what unit you get when you divide an energy unit by a charge unit.
Compare coulomb per second for current and joule per second for power with joule per coulomb to see which matches energy divided by charge.
walkthrough: Identify what the volt measures: potential difference $V$, the energy transferred per unit charge passing between two points.
State the governing definition: $V = W/Q$, where $W$ is work done or energy transferred and $Q$ is charge.
Insert SI units: $W$ is in joules $\text{J}$ and $Q$ is in coulombs $\text{C}$, so $V$ is in $\text{J C}^{-1}$.
Hence one volt means one joule of energy per one coulomb of charge: $1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J C}^{-1}$.
Check the distractors: coulomb per second is the ampere and joule per second is the watt, so they do not fit $W/Q$.

A.explanation: One coulomb per second is charge per unit time, which defines the ampere for current $I = Q/t$, not the volt.

B.explanation: Potential difference is energy per unit charge $V = W/Q$, so $1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J C}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: One joule per second is energy per unit time, which defines the watt for power $P = W/t$, not the volt.

D.explanation: Joule second per coulomb squared does not match $W/Q$ and has different base-unit dimensions from potential difference.
